claim: 54% of cells in mouse ADn meet the HD selection criterion
source: (C) Pie charts showing that 54% of cells in mouse ADn meet the HD selection criterion, but only 12% in RSC do (right) (n=12 mice, 9 with simultaneous ADn and RSC, 2 ADn only and 2 RSC only).
evidence: Based on experimental data from recordings in 12 mice, with specific HD cell selection criteria applied

claim: 12% of cells in mouse RSC meet the HD selection criterion
source: (C) Pie charts showing that 54% of cells in mouse ADn meet the HD selection criterion, but only 12% in RSC do (right) (n=12 mice, 9 with simultaneous ADn and RSC, 2 ADn only and 2 RSC only).
evidence: Based on experimental data from recordings in 12 mice, with specific HD cell selection criteria applied

claim: Directional information in RSC HD cells is lower than in ADn HD cells
source: directional information in RSC was lower than in ADn (bits/spike, median: ADn HD = 0.084, n=150; RSC HD = 0.015, n=73; ADn non-HD=0.011, n=122; RSC non-HD=0.006, n=584; Kruskal-Wallis test p<0.0001, p<0.0001 for multiple comparisons, except for ADn nonHD versus RSC HD p>0.05, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Statistical comparison of directional information between ADn and RSC HD cells using Kruskal-Wallis test

claim: The median resultant length is higher in ADn HD cells than RSC HD cells
source: as well as the median resultant length (median: ADn HD = 0.21, n=150; RSC HD = 0.084, n=73; ADn non-HD=0.047, n=122; RSC non-HD=0.041, n=584; Kruskal-Wallis test p<0.0001, p<0.0001 for multiple comparisons, except for ADn versus RSC HD, p=0.0031, and nonHD, p=0.028, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: Statistical comparison of resultant length between ADn and RSC HD cells using Kruskal-Wallis test

claim: The preferred direction difference between pairs of ADn HD neurons remained rigid after cue rotations
source: As expected, the preferred direction difference between pairs of ADn HD neurons remained rigid after cue rotations (Figure 1F, circular correlation = 0.91, n=603 pairs, 10 mice).
evidence: Circular correlation analysis of preferred direction differences in ADn HD cell pairs before and after cue rotation

claim: RSC HD cells show a significant but smaller correlation in preferred direction difference after cue rotations compared to ADn
source: In RSC HD cells, we observed a smaller yet significant correlation (0.28, n=269 pairs, 9 mice) in the preferred direction difference of RSC HD pairs between before and after cue rotations (Figure 1G).
evidence: Circular correlation analysis of preferred direction differences in RSC HD cell pairs before and after cue rotation

claim: RSC's preferred firing directions were significantly stable although less than ADn HD units
source: We found that RSC's PFDs were significantly stable although less than ADn HD units (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F, ADn left n=150, correlation = 0.93, RSC right n=73, correlation = 0.79, p<0.0001 for both).
evidence: Correlation analysis of preferred firing directions between two consecutive segments with stable cue orientation

claim: The strength of HD tuning did not change between two sample trials across RSC HD cells
source: Furthermore, the strength of HD tuning, quantified as the resultant, did not change between two sample trials from selected significant cue rotation sessions across RSC HD cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G right, n=71, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test p=0.79, median before = 0.086, after = 0.088)
evidence: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test comparing resultant values before and after cue rotation in RSC HD cells

claim: The strength of HD tuning did not change between two sample trials across ADn HD cells
source: Furthermore, the strength of HD tuning, quantified as the resultant, did not change between two sample trials from selected significant cue rotation sessions across RSC HD cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G right, n=71, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test p=0.79, median before = 0.086, after = 0.088) as well as ADn HD cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G left, n=128, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test p=0.23, median before = 0.22, after = 0.23).
evidence: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test comparing resultant values before and after cue rotation in ADn HD cells

claim: The rotations from simultaneously recorded ADn and RSC HD ensembles were more correlated than those produced by random shifting
source: Despite a bias toward the inertial (self-motion-driven) HD estimate, evident through the higher density of rotations around 0, the rotations from simultaneously recorded ADn and RSC HD ensembles were more correlated (coefficient = 0.54 from unique ensembles for different sizes and directions of rotations, 7 mice) than those produced by random shifting of RSC and ADn neural activity around the cue rotations (Figure 1H).
evidence: Circular correlation analysis comparing real data to shuffled controls

claim: The median decoded error from the test period was 36.32° in ADn and 47.53° in RSC
source: From the remaining sessions, the median decoded error from the test period was 36.32° in ADn (n=36 unique ensembles) and 47.53° in RSC (n=29 ensembles) (p=0.0039, Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Mann-Whitney test comparing median decoded errors between ADn and RSC

claim: Decoding performance dropped for high compared to low angular velocity
source: Indeed, decoding performance dropped for high compared to low angular velocity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F), (low angular velocity medians: ADn = 33.4°, RSC = 43.4°, high angular velocity medians: ADn = 39.4°, RSC = 60.9°).
evidence: Comparison of decoding accuracy at different angular velocity states

claim: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant differences in decoding accuracy between ADn and RSC
source: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant differences between the two regions (p<0.0001) and also between the two velocity states (p=0.0012), but no effect for the interaction between the two variables (p>0.05), suggesting that the angular velocity effect was largely similar between the two regions.
evidence: Two-way ANOVA statistical test on decoding accuracy data

claim: The errors from the GLM decoder reflected the mean rotations of the ensemble HD neurons tuning curves in both ADn and RSC
source: The errors from our GLM decoder reflected the mean rotations of the ensemble HD neurons tuning curves both from ADn and RSC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H, 0.73 and 0.75 circular correlation coefficients for ADn, n=113, and RSC, n=59 unique ensembles for different sizes and directions of rotations, respectively, p<0.0001 for both)
evidence: Circular correlation analysis between decoded errors and mean tuning curve rotations

claim: The mean decoded errors after cue rotations from simultaneously recorded ADn and RSC ensembles were correlated
source: The mean decoded errors after cue rotations from simultaneously recorded ADn and RSC ensembles were also correlated (Figure 2B, 0.74 circular correlation coefficient, n=95 unique ensembles for different sizes and directions of rotations, from 8 mice)
evidence: Circular correlation analysis of decoded errors between simultaneously recorded ADn and RSC ensembles

claim: The two regions were synchronized within 20ms in HD reference update
source: Contrary to our predictions (i.e. that RSC would lead the HD reference update via visual integration of the cue's new angular position), we found that the two regions were synchronized (within 20ms) in this regard.
evidence: Temporal cross-correlation analysis of decoded errors between ADn and RSC

claim: HD cells maintained the same initial preferred directions while the cue was on in a stable position, but were more variable while the cue was off
source: HD cells maintained the same initial preferred directions while the cue was on in a stable position, but were more variable while the cue was off, and sometimes continuously drifted during prolonged darkness (Figure 3B).
evidence: Observation of HD cell behavior during cue-on and cue-off conditions

claim: The mean firing rates of the recorded ensembles were stable between cue-on and -off conditions in ADn
source: The mean firing rates of the recorded ensembles were stable between cue-on and -off conditions in ADn (n=155, p=0.067 Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test)
evidence: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test comparing mean firing rates between cue-on and cue-off conditions in ADn

claim: The mean firing rates of the recorded ensembles were marginally reduced in RSC between cue-on and cue-off conditions
source: The mean firing rates of the recorded ensembles were stable between cue-on and -off conditions in ADn (n=155, p=0.067 Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test) and marginally reduced in RSC (n=159, p=0.046)
evidence: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test comparing mean firing rates between cue-on and cue-off conditions in RSC

claim: The peak firing rates of HD cells in both ADn and RSC were reduced in darkness
source: The peak firing rates of HD cells both in ADn and RSC were reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 3I, ADn n=91 median cue-on 62.52 Hz, cue-off 57.63 Hz, p=0.0027, RSC n=27 median cue-on 41.36 Hz, cue-off 37.74 Hz, p=0.0004, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test)
evidence: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test comparing peak firing rates between cue-on and cue-off conditions

claim: Only RSC's HD resultant lengths were affected by darkness
source: but only RSC's HD resultant lengths were affected by darkness (Figure 1—figure supplement 3J, cue-on median 0.123, cue-off median 0.087, p=0.0057 for RSC, cue-on median 0.22, cue-off median 0.21, p=0.69 for ADn)
evidence: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test comparing resultant lengths between cue-on and cue-off conditions

claim: Modest levels of drift were observed in darkness
source: On average, we observed modest levels of drift in darkness (Figure 3F, n=15 ADn ensembles from 58 trials, p=0.0053 Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test between cue-on drift, median = 15.9°, and cue-off drift, median = 25.6°).
evidence: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test comparing drift between cue-on and cue-off conditions

claim: Correlated HD representations were observed between ADn and RSC both during cue-on and cue-off periods
source: When we applied the same decoding strategy as in the rotation trials to quantify the drift in the two regions, we observed correlated HD representations between ADn and RSC both during cue-on and cue-off periods (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Decoding analysis showing correlation between ADn and RSC HD representations in both light conditions

claim: The circular correlations of the decoded drifts were similar between cue-on and cue-off periods
source: The circular correlations of the decoded drifts were similar between cue-on (r=0.277) and cue-off periods (r=0.256) (p=0.677, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test, n=12 unique ensembles) and were significantly higher than the correlations with shuffled RSC drifts (Figure 3D&E, right)
evidence: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test comparing circular correlations between cue-on and cue-off periods

claim: RSC cells from the same areas where tetrode recordings were performed received dense anterior thalamic inputs, particularly from ADn
source: We found that RSC cells from the same areas where we performed tetrode recordings (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B) received dense anterior thalamic inputs, and particularly ADn (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Retrograde monosynaptic rabies tracing experiments showing anatomical connectivity

claim: ADn exhibited surprisingly sparse presynaptic RSC cell labeling
source: Conversely, ADn exhibited surprisingly sparse presynaptic RSC cell labeling.
evidence: Retrograde monosynaptic rabies tracing experiments showing anatomical connectivity

claim: Presynaptic RSC cells to ADn were frequently localized in the granular and ventral portion of RSC
source: These cells were frequently localized in the granular and ventral portion of RSC (Figure 4B).
evidence: Anatomical localization from retrograde tracing experiments

claim: 6.88% of all possible ADn-RSC pairs had a monosynaptic connection in the ADn-to-RSC direction
source: Using this metric (Peyrache et al., 2015; Stark and Abeles, 2009), we identified 6.88% of all possible pairs with a monosynaptic connection in the ADn-to-RSC direction (348 out of 5056)
evidence: Spike cross-correlation analysis identifying putative monosynaptic connections

claim: Only 0.08% of all possible pairs had a monosynaptic connection in the RSC-to-ADn direction
source: Using this metric (Peyrache et al., 2015; Stark and Abeles, 2009), we identified 6.88% of all possible pairs with a monosynaptic connection in the ADn-to-RSC direction (348 out of 5056) and only 0.08% in the RSC-to-ADn direction (4 out of 5056).
evidence: Spike cross-correlation analysis identifying putative monosynaptic connections

claim: 91 out of 326 ADn units had at least one connection to RSC
source: In terms of unit counts, 91 out of 326 ADn units had at least one connection to RSC, while only 4 out of 749 RSC units had a connection with ADn (Figure 4D).
evidence: Quantification of functional connectivity from spike cross-correlation analysis

claim: Only 4 out of 749 RSC units had a connection with ADn
source: In terms of unit counts, 91 out of 326 ADn units had at least one connection to RSC, while only 4 out of 749 RSC units had a connection with ADn (Figure 4D).
evidence: Quantification of functional connectivity from spike cross-correlation analysis

claim: The mean number of RSC synaptic partners was 4.23 for ADn HD cells and 0.04 for non-HD cells
source: The mean number of RSC synaptic partners was 4.23 for ADn HD cells and 0.04 for non-HD cells.
evidence: Quantification of synaptic connectivity from spike cross-correlation analysis

claim: ADn's dense connectivity largely originated from identified HD cells
source: ADn's dense connectivity largely originated from identified HD cells (275 connected pairs from ADn HD cells versus 72 from non-HD ADn cells) and included both HD as well as non-HD partner cells in RSC (Figure 4F).
evidence: Quantification of connectivity patterns by cell type from spike cross-correlation analysis

claim: The distribution of the preferred direction differences between ADn HD-coding units and their HD-coding synaptic partners in RSC showed a small but significant bias toward similar tuning
source: Finally, the distribution of the preferred direction differences between ADn HD-coding units and their HD-coding synaptic partners in RSC showed a small but significant bias toward similar tuning (Figure 4G left polar plot, n=73 units, 28 RS and 47 FS, 6 mice, circular mean –5.4° with a circular standard deviation of 61°, Rayleigh test for non-uniformity p=0.005 for the RS synaptic partners only, p=0.002 when both cell types were combined).
evidence: Rayleigh test for non-uniformity of preferred direction differences between connected HD cells

claim: The preferred direction differences between ADn units and all other non-synaptically connected HD-coding units showed a uniform distribution
source: This similarity bias was not observed for the preferred direction differences between the same ADn units and all other non-synaptically connected HD-coding units, whose distribution was uniform (Figure 4G right polar plot, n=73, 65 RS and 8 FS units, Rayleigh test p=0.052 for the RS units, p=0.086 for RS and FS combined).
evidence: Rayleigh test for uniformity of preferred direction differences between non-connected HD cells

claim: The sense of direction is critical for survival in changing environments and relies on flexibly integrating self-motion signals with external sensory cues
source: The sense of direction is critical for survival in changing environments and relies on flexibly integrating self-motion signals with external sensory cues.
evidence: General statement about the importance of directional sense, drawing from established scientific understanding

claim: Retrosplenial cortex (RSC) plays a key role in forming coherent representations of space in mammals
source: Retrosplenial cortex (RSC) plays a key role in forming coherent representations of space in mammals and it encodes a variety of navigational variables, including HD.
evidence: General statement about RSC function, drawing from established scientific literature

claim: RSC encodes a variety of navigational variables, including HD
source: Retrosplenial cortex (RSC) plays a key role in forming coherent representations of space in mammals and it encodes a variety of navigational variables, including HD.
evidence: General statement about RSC encoding properties, drawing from established scientific literature

claim: ADn is the obligatory thalamic relay of HD to cortex
source: the anterodorsal nucleus of thalamus (ADn), the obligatory thalamic relay of HD to cortex
evidence: General statement about ADn function, drawing from established scientific literature

claim: Coordination of HD representations in ADn and RSC is maintained during darkness
source: Moreover, coordination of HD representations in the two regions is maintained during darkness.
evidence: Summary statement of experimental findings from cue-off experiments

claim: Anatomical and functional connectivity are consistent with a strong feedforward drive of HD information from ADn to RSC
source: We further show that anatomical and functional connectivity are consistent with a strong feedforward drive of HD information from ADn to RSC, with anatomically restricted corticothalamic feedback.
evidence: Summary statement of anatomical tracing and functional connectivity findings

claim: There is anatomically restricted corticothalamic feedback from RSC to ADn
source: We further show that anatomical and functional connectivity are consistent with a strong feedforward drive of HD information from ADn to RSC, with anatomically restricted corticothalamic feedback.
evidence: Summary statement of anatomical tracing findings

claim: The results indicate a concerted global HD reference update across cortex and thalamus
source: Together, our results indicate a concerted global HD reference update across cortex and thalamus.
evidence: Summary interpretation of experimental findings on HD coordination

claim: Changes in environmental information trigger remapping of place cells
source: Changes in environmental information are known to trigger remapping of place (Muller and Kubie, 1987), grid (Fyhn et al., 2007) and realignment of HD receptive fields (Taube, 1990; Goodridge et al., 1998; Knierim et al., 1998).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Changes in environmental information trigger remapping of grid cells
source: Changes in environmental information are known to trigger remapping of place (Muller and Kubie, 1987), grid (Fyhn et al., 2007) and realignment of HD receptive fields (Taube, 1990; Goodridge et al., 1998; Knierim et al., 1998).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Changes in environmental information trigger realignment of HD receptive fields
source: Changes in environmental information are known to trigger remapping of place (Muller and Kubie, 1987), grid (Fyhn et al., 2007) and realignment of HD receptive fields (Taube, 1990; Goodridge et al., 1998; Knierim et al., 1998).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Visual cues influence the HD signal by providing an external anchoring reference
source: Visual cues influence the HD signal by providing an external anchoring reference (Taube, 1990; Taube and Burton, 1995), counteracting the drift from stochastic error in angular velocity integration observed in darkness (Mizumori and Williams, 1993; Stackman and Taube, 1997; Valerio and Taube, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Visual cues counteract the drift from stochastic error in angular velocity integration observed in darkness
source: Visual cues influence the HD signal by providing an external anchoring reference (Taube, 1990; Taube and Burton, 1995), counteracting the drift from stochastic error in angular velocity integration observed in darkness (Mizumori and Williams, 1993; Stackman and Taube, 1997; Valerio and Taube, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Realignment has been observed in the form of rotations of preferred firing directions of HD cells in response to rotations of a prominent visual cue
source: In the insect and mammalian HD systems, realignment has been observed in the form of rotations of preferred firing directions (PFD) of HD cells in response to rotations of a prominent visual cue - often a color-contrast card (Taube, 1990; Goodridge et al., 1998), a narrow band (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015) or scene (Kim et al., 2019) on an LED screen.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research in both insect and mammalian systems

claim: Hebbian synaptic plasticity mechanisms have been proposed to explain realignment phenomena in the fly ellipsoid body
source: Hebbian synaptic plasticity mechanisms, acting in specific circuit arrangements, have been proposed to explain these phenomena in the fly ellipsoid body (Fisher et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Network models with similar architecture to fly ellipsoid body have been applied to the rodent HD system
source: Network models with similar architecture have been applied to the rodent HD system (Hahnloser, 2003; Knight et al., 2014; Page et al., 2014; Skaggs et al., 1995).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous modeling studies

claim: The circuitry that drives HD realignment in the rodent brain is not yet resolved
source: However, unlike the fly brain (Franconville et al., 2018; Hanesch et al., 1989), the circuitry that drives HD realignment in the rodent brain is not yet resolved.
evidence: Statement contrasting known fly circuitry with unknown rodent circuitry, supported by citations

claim: Several studies have indicated that cortical regions play a role in the stability and the visual anchoring of HD cells
source: Several studies have indicated that cortical regions play a role in the stability and the visual anchoring of HD cells (Clark et al., 2010; Golob and Taube, 1999; Goodridge and Taube, 1997)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: It is unknown whether the HD representation is first aligned to the sensory cues in cortex and then updated in downstream regions
source: but whether the HD representation is first aligned to the sensory cues in cortex and then updated in downstream regions is still unknown.
evidence: Statement identifying a gap in current knowledge

claim: ADn is the necessary thalamic relay of HD to the hippocampal formation and cortex
source: Previous studies in the rat indicate that the HD code in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus (ADn), the necessary thalamic relay of HD to the hippocampal formation and cortex (Calton et al., 2003; Frost et al., 2021; Goodridge and Taube, 1997; Jenkins et al., 2004; Winter et al., 2015)
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research

claim: The HD code in ADn becomes unstable and is less likely to remap to reflect cue rotations after lesions to the retrosplenial cortex
source: Previous studies in the rat indicate that the HD code in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus (ADn), the necessary thalamic relay of HD to the hippocampal formation and cortex (Calton et al., 2003; Frost et al., 2021; Goodridge and Taube, 1997; Jenkins et al., 2004; Winter et al., 2015), becomes unstable and is less likely to remap to reflect cue rotations after lesions to the retrosplenial cortex (RSC; Clark et al., 2010)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous lesion study

claim: The HD code in ADn becomes unstable and is less likely to remap to reflect cue rotations after lesions to the post-subiculum
source: Previous studies in the rat indicate that the HD code in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus (ADn), the necessary thalamic relay of HD to the hippocampal formation and cortex (Calton et al., 2003; Frost et al., 2021; Goodridge and Taube, 1997; Jenkins et al., 2004; Winter et al., 2015), becomes unstable and is less likely to remap to reflect cue rotations after lesions to the retrosplenial cortex (RSC; Clark et al., 2010) or the post-subiculum (POS; Goodridge and Taube, 1997).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous lesion study

claim: RSC and POS are strongly interconnected with visual areas
source: Both of these regions are strongly interconnected with visual areas (Sugar et al., 2011; Van Groen and Wyss, 2003), with each other (Kononenko and Witter, 2012; Wyss and Van Groen, 1992), and with ADn (Jankowski et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous anatomical studies

claim: RSC and POS are strongly interconnected with each other
source: Both of these regions are strongly interconnected with visual areas (Sugar et al., 2011; Van Groen and Wyss, 2003), with each other (Kononenko and Witter, 2012; Wyss and Van Groen, 1992), and with ADn (Jankowski et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous anatomical studies

claim: RSC and POS are strongly interconnected with ADn
source: Both of these regions are strongly interconnected with visual areas (Sugar et al., 2011; Van Groen and Wyss, 2003), with each other (Kononenko and Witter, 2012; Wyss and Van Groen, 1992), and with ADn (Jankowski et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous anatomical studies

claim: HD dominates the spatial code in POS
source: While HD dominates the spatial code in POS (Taube, 1990; Peyrache et al., 2017; Laurens et al., 2019)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: RSC exhibits diverse visuo-spatial activity
source: RSC exhibits diverse visuo-spatial activity (Cho and Sharp, 2001; Fischer et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2017; Powell et al., 2020; Voigts and Harnett, 2020)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: RSC has complex receptive fields shaped by multiple spatial correlates
source: RSC exhibits diverse visuo-spatial activity (Cho and Sharp, 2001; Fischer et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2017; Powell et al., 2020; Voigts and Harnett, 2020), with complex receptive fields shaped by multiple spatial correlates (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2017; Jacob et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: POS presents mostly homogeneous, cue-guided rotations of HD fields in response to rotations of a prominent visual cue
source: Unlike POS, which presents mostly homogeneous, cue-guided rotations of HD fields in response to rotations of a prominent visual cue (Taube, 1990)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research

claim: Diverse responses of RSC HD cells to cue manipulations or specific environmental configurations have been reported
source: diverse responses of RSC HD cells to cue manipulations or specific environmental configurations have been reported (Chen et al., 1994a; Jacob et al., 2017; Sit and Goard, 2023)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: RSC plays a critical role in spatial cognition
source: As a cortical association area, RSC plays a critical role in spatial cognition (Knight and Hayman, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2018; Vann et al., 2009) and spatial memory (Miller et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2014)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: RSC plays a critical role in spatial memory
source: As a cortical association area, RSC plays a critical role in spatial cognition (Knight and Hayman, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2018; Vann et al., 2009) and spatial memory (Miller et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2014)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Rats and humans with RSC lesions show impairments in route planning
source: rats and humans with RSC lesions show impairments in route planning as well as identification and flexible use of navigational landmarks (Hindley et al., 2014; Maguire, 2001; Pothuizen et al., 2008; Vann and Aggleton, 2004).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous lesion studies

claim: Rats and humans with RSC lesions show impairments in identification and flexible use of navigational landmarks
source: rats and humans with RSC lesions show impairments in route planning as well as identification and flexible use of navigational landmarks (Hindley et al., 2014; Maguire, 2001; Pothuizen et al., 2008; Vann and Aggleton, 2004).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous lesion studies

claim: In the intact RSC, associations between egocentric and allocentric reference frames become evident with spatial tasks
source: Specifically, in the intact RSC, associations between egocentric and allocentric reference frames become evident with spatial tasks (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Shine and Wolbers, 2021; van Wijngaarden et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: RSC is necessary for path integration-based navigation in darkness
source: Moreover, RSC is also necessary for path integration-based navigation in darkness (Elduayen and Save, 2014)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research

claim: The coordination between POS and ADn HD representations has been elucidated across wake and sleep states
source: However, while the coordination between POS and ADn HD representations has been already elucidated across wake and sleep states (Peyrache et al., 2015)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research

claim: It is unknown how visually-guided changes in HD representation are coordinated between RSC and ADn
source: it is unknown how visually-guided changes in HD representation are coordinated between RSC and ADn.
evidence: Statement identifying a gap in current knowledge

claim: The differences between ADn and RSC HD encoding were consistent with the higher degree of multi-modal selectivity in RSC
source: The differences between these two regions were consistent with a the higher degree of multi-modal selectivity in RSC (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Cho and Sharp, 2001; Laurens et al., 2019), where multiple spatial correlates, contexts and states are mixed with and influence HD coding.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and citations to previous research

claim: In RSC, multiple spatial correlates, contexts and states are mixed with and influence HD coding
source: The differences between these two regions were consistent with a the higher degree of multi-modal selectivity in RSC (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Cho and Sharp, 2001; Laurens et al., 2019), where multiple spatial correlates, contexts and states are mixed with and influence HD coding.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: The HD map is well-locked between ADn and RSC in the behavioral paradigm used
source: This suggested that the HD map is well-locked between the two regions in our behavioral paradigm, despite the differences in HD encoding between ADn and RSC.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing correlation between ADn and RSC rotations

claim: Large mismatches between cue position and internal HD were more likely to result in under-rotations
source: This suggested that even though large mismatches were more likely to result in under-rotations, we could pool the results of the rotation analyses.
evidence: Inference based on analysis of rotation data as a function of rotation size

claim: The initial egocentric experience of the cue rotation was not a factor in the under-rotations of the HD representation in the behavioral setting used
source: Altogether, these analyses indicate that, in our behavioral setting, the initial egocentric experience of the cue rotation was not a factor in the under-rotations of the HD representation.
evidence: Conclusion based on analysis of egocentric cue position and rotation magnitude

claim: Variable and mostly slow HD reference shifts were observed in both ADn and RSC
source: By applying our decoding strategy, we first observed that decoded errors drifted to a new HD reference at a variable speed (Figure 2C). On average we observed similar, and mostly slow, HD reference shifts in both ADn and RSC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: Observation from decoding analysis of HD representations

claim: The majority of trials had cross-correlation peaks at 0ms time lags both before and after cue rotations
source: While some trial-to-trial variability in the correlation level was observed, the majority of trials had peaks at 0ms time lags (two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test between data and null distribution, p<0.0001 for both stable and shifted), both before and after cue rotations (Figure 2D and E; Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test p=0.88, n=28 unique ensembles from 108 trials).
evidence: Statistical analysis of temporal cross-correlations between ADn and RSC decoded errors

claim: The two regions were coordinated even in the initial stages of the shifting of the HD representation
source: This confirmed that the two regions were coordinated even in the initial stages of the shifting of the HD representation.
evidence: Conclusion based on temporal cross-correlation analysis

claim: The HD representation is coordinated between ADn and RSC in the absence of a visual input
source: Our results therefore indicate that the HD representation is also coordinated between ADn and RSC in the absence of a visual input, but can be challenged during periods of HD instability.
evidence: Conclusion based on analysis of cue-off trials

claim: HD coordination between ADn and RSC can be challenged during periods of HD instability
source: Our results therefore indicate that the HD representation is also coordinated between ADn and RSC in the absence of a visual input, but can be challenged during periods of HD instability.
evidence: Conclusion based on analysis of high angular velocity periods during cue-off

claim: The anatomical findings are consistent with previous studies in the rat
source: Overall, these results are consistent with previous studies in the rat (Shibata, 1998; Shibata, 1993; van Groen and Wyss, 1990a; Vantomme et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison of current anatomical findings with previous research

claim: ADn sustains the RSC HD code with a widespread feedforward connectivity to both RS and FS units
source: Together, these results suggest that ADn sustains the RSC HD code with a widespread feedforward connectivity to both RS and FS units, a connectivity that targets not only HD-tuned units, directly shaping their preferred directions (Figure 4H), but also units with more complex, presumably multimodal, receptive fields.
evidence: Inference based on functional connectivity analysis and preferred direction similarity

claim: ADn connectivity targets not only HD-tuned units in RSC, directly shaping their preferred directions, but also units with more complex, presumably multimodal, receptive fields
source: Together, these results suggest that ADn sustains the RSC HD code with a widespread feedforward connectivity to both RS and FS units, a connectivity that targets not only HD-tuned units, directly shaping their preferred directions (Figure 4H), but also units with more complex, presumably multimodal, receptive fields.
evidence: Inference based on functional connectivity analysis showing connections to both HD and non-HD units

claim: The very sparse RSC-to-ADn connections are unlikely to drive the change or the stability in preferred directions in ADn
source: On the other hand, the very sparse RSC-to-ADn connections that we identified are, alone, unlikely to drive the change or the stability, in the presence of visual cues, in preferred directions in ADn (Figure 4I).
evidence: Inference based on the very low number of RSC-to-ADn connections identified

claim: The HD representation in ADn and RSC is closely coordinated in conditions when visual cues are stable
source: Our data show that the HD representation in ADn and RSC is closely coordinated, both in conditions when visual cues are stable and during adaptation to a new reference in response to cue rotation (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from stable cue periods

claim: The HD representation in ADn and RSC is closely coordinated during adaptation to a new reference in response to cue rotation
source: Our data show that the HD representation in ADn and RSC is closely coordinated, both in conditions when visual cues are stable and during adaptation to a new reference in response to cue rotation (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from cue rotation trials

claim: Visual input is not necessary for maintaining coordinated HD representations between ADn and RSC
source: This is also true for HD drift in darkness (Figure 3D, E and G), showing that visual input is not necessary for maintaining these coordinated representations, and that other sensory modalities, such as angular velocity, optic flow, and/or motor efference copy, influence ADn and RSC HD.
evidence: Conclusion based on analysis of cue-off trials showing maintained coordination

claim: Other sensory modalities, such as angular velocity, optic flow, and/or motor efference copy, influence ADn and RSC HD
source: This is also true for HD drift in darkness (Figure 3D, E and G), showing that visual input is not necessary for maintaining these coordinated representations, and that other sensory modalities, such as angular velocity, optic flow, and/or motor efference copy, influence ADn and RSC HD.
evidence: Inference based on maintained coordination in darkness and known sources of HD information

claim: Functional connectivity supports the ADn-RSC HD coordination through a strong feedforward input to RSC
source: Finally, our functional connectivity (Figure 4D) supports the ADn-RSC HD coordination through a strong feedforward input to RSC, which shapes the local HD code there (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Summary of functional connectivity findings

claim: The bias toward similar tuning between connected ADn and RSC HD units suggests that ADn HD code might not be simply inherited in RSC
source: Specifically, the bias toward similar tuning between connected ADn and RSC HD units suggests that ADn HD code might not be simply inherited in RSC, as has been shown in POS (Peyrache et al., 2015; Peyrache et al., 2017), but likely integrated with other spatial codes via different circuit organization principles, that include recruitment of FS and RS neurons (Simonnet et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on preferred direction similarity analysis and comparison with POS, supported by citations

claim: ADn HD code is likely integrated with other spatial codes in RSC via different circuit organization principles that include recruitment of FS and RS neurons
source: Specifically, the bias toward similar tuning between connected ADn and RSC HD units suggests that ADn HD code might not be simply inherited in RSC, as has been shown in POS (Peyrache et al., 2015; Peyrache et al., 2017), but likely integrated with other spatial codes via different circuit organization principles, that include recruitment of FS and RS neurons (Simonnet et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on connectivity patterns to both HD and non-HD units, supported by citation

claim: The visually driven updating of the internal HD is a more complex process that privileges coordination across brain regions over sustained error signals with mismatched representations
source: We conclude that the visually driven updating of the internal HD is a more complex process that privileges coordination across brain regions over sustained error signals with mismatched representations.
evidence: Conclusion based on the finding of synchronous HD updates rather than temporal offsets

claim: The temporal resolution of the decoding occludes potential faster dynamics at the scale of monosynaptic connections
source: However, the temporal resolution of the decoding occludes potential faster dynamics, at the scale of monosynaptic connections (ms range).
evidence: Acknowledgment of methodological limitation

claim: Slow, continuous drifts of the HD representation after cue rotation have been observed in flies
source: Slow, continuous drifts of the HD representation after cue rotation as reported here (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3H) have also been observed in flies (Kim, 2017)
evidence: Comparison of current findings with previous research in flies

claim: Slow, continuous drifts of the HD representation after cue rotation have been observed in rat ADn
source: Slow, continuous drifts of the HD representation after cue rotation as reported here (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3H) have also been observed in flies (Kim, 2017) and in rat (Knierim et al., 1998) and mouse (Ajabi et al., 2023) ADn
evidence: Comparison of current findings with previous research in rats

claim: Slow, continuous drifts of the HD representation after cue rotation have been observed in mouse ADn
source: Slow, continuous drifts of the HD representation after cue rotation as reported here (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3H) have also been observed in flies (Kim, 2017) and in rat (Knierim et al., 1998) and mouse (Ajabi et al., 2023) ADn
evidence: Comparison of current findings with previous research in mice

claim: One study in rat ADn observed immediate HD shifting in specific cue-heading configurations
source: with the exception of one study in the rat ADn (Zugaro et al., 2003) where immediate HD shifting was observed in specific cue-heading configurations.
evidence: Citation to previous research showing different results

claim: Repeated exposure to an unstable cue is known to cause landmark devaluation
source: Repeated exposure to an unstable cue is known to cause landmark devaluation (Knierim et al., 1995; Knight and Hayman, 2014)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Extended navigation within the same environment increased the incidence of under- or 0° rotations in the data
source: Repeated exposure to an unstable cue is known to cause landmark devaluation (Knierim et al., 1995; Knight and Hayman, 2014) and, together with extended navigation within the same environment, increased the incidence of under- or 0° rotations in our data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Observation from experimental data analysis

claim: POS could provide the visual reference information to ADn, RSC and LMN through its reciprocal connections with visual areas
source: POS, through its reciprocal connections with visual areas, could provide the visual reference information to ADn, RSC and LMN, the obligatory HD path upstream of ADn (Yoder et al., 2015; Yoder and Taube, 2011).
evidence: Speculation about circuit mechanisms supported by citations

claim: Another possible route for visual-HD integration includes the cortico-thalamic control through thalamic reticular nucleus
source: Another possible route includes the cortico-thalamic control through thalamic reticular nucleus, which readily and densely inhibits ADn and receives presubicular and retrosplenial connections (Vantomme et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation about circuit mechanisms supported by citation

claim: The asymmetry in ADn-RSC connectivity was more extreme than that observed in previously reported ADn-POS connectivity
source: This asymmetry was more extreme than that observed in previously reported ADn-POS connectivity (Peyrache et al., 2015; van Groen and Wyss, 1990b)
evidence: Comparison of current findings with previous research

claim: The extreme asymmetry in connectivity was possibly exacerbated by the widespread sampling of RSC locations in the recordings
source: and possibly exacerbated by the widespread sampling of RSC locations in our recordings, across granular and dysgranular portions, with a higher concentration of tetrodes in the upper L2/3 and L5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and 9 out of 48 cortical tetrodes in mice with simultaneous ADn and RSC recordings in L6.
evidence: Speculation about methodological factors affecting results

claim: RSC displays a gradient along the anterior-posterior axis in encoding egocentric versus allocentric navigational variables
source: Given that RSC displays a gradient along the anterior-posterior axis in encoding egocentric versus allocentric navigational variables (Hennestad et al., 2021)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research

claim: RSC is necessary for ADn HD alignment to visual cues
source: In fact, RSC is necessary for ADn HD alignment to visual cues (Clark et al., 2010)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous lesion study

claim: The dense interconnection between RSC and several regions of the hippocampal formation may support coordinated HD representation across the brain
source: and the dense interconnection between RSC and several regions of the hippocampal formation (Sugar et al., 2011; Wyss and Van Groen, 1992) may support coordinated HD representation across the brain as a mechanism to ensure consistent flexible spatial computations relevant to behavior output.
evidence: Speculation about functional implications supported by citations
